issues.legal_issue: A tenant must pay the costs of the suit, in addition to the rent due, to obtain protection against eviction under the statutory rent-payment provision.
material_facts: In an eviction suit for non-payment of rent, the standard rent was fixed during the suit, and the tenant paid the arrears calculated at that rent.
The trial court directed the tenant to pay the suit costs, but the tenant did not pay them and admitted being unable to tender them.
The appellate court held that the eviction suit fell within the statutory provision requiring payment of costs, and the High Court dismissed the tenant’s revision.
issues.conclusion: The tenant was not entitled to protection against eviction because the tenant had not paid or tendered the suit costs as required.
issues.legal_principle: Section 12(3)(b) of the Bombay Rent Act requires a tenant seeking protection from an eviction decree to pay or tender the rent due and, as directed by the court, the costs of the suit. A tenant who fails to comply with that requirement is not entitled to the protection. No earlier cases are cited.

rule.if: rent_default_eviction_suit and tenant_paid_rent_arrears and tenant_failed_to_pay_suit_costs and tenant_admitted_inability_to_tender_costs

predicates.rent_default_eviction_suit: The landlord brought an eviction suit alleging the tenant's failure to pay rent.
predicates.tenant_paid_rent_arrears: The tenant paid the rent arrears due by the relevant hearing.
predicates.tenant_failed_to_pay_suit_costs: The tenant did not pay or tender the suit costs directed by the court.
predicates.tenant_admitted_inability_to_tender_cost: The tenant told the trial court that the tenant was unable to tender the suit costs.
predicates.tenant_not_entitled_to_rent_protection_a: The tenant is not entitled to statutory protection against eviction.

issues.definition: When an eviction suit is brought for rent default, payment of the arrears does not secure rent protection if the tenant fails to pay the suit costs and admits being unable to tender them.

issues.legal_issue: The Supreme Court will not interfere with a High Court’s discretionary decision on the basis of a material fact that was not brought to the High Court’s attention.
material_facts: The High Court dismissed the tenant’s revision and later heard and dismissed a review application.

The tenant alleged in the Supreme Court that the suit costs had been paid after the appeal was filed, but that alleged payment had not been brought to the High Court’s attention when it considered the matter.
The High Court had exercised its discretion on the facts and circumstances presented to it.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court would not interfere with the High Court’s exercise of discretion on the basis of the alleged payment that had not been brought to the High Court’s attention.
issues.legal_principle: An appellate court should not substitute its discretion for that of the High Court on the basis of facts that were never presented to the High Court. No statutory provision or earlier case is cited for this point.

predicates.appeal_reviewing_high_court_discretion: The proceeding is an appeal asking the Supreme Court to review a discretionary decision made by the High Court.
predicates.material_fact_alleged_on_appeal_not_pres: A party relies on appeal on a material fact that was not brought to the High Court’s attention when it made its decision.
predicates.supreme_court_does_not_interfere_with_hi: The Supreme Court does not interfere with the High Court’s discretionary decision on the basis of a material fact not presented to it.

issues.definition: When an appeal seeks review of the High Court’s discretion and relies on a material fact not presented to that court, the Supreme Court does not interfere with that discretion on that basis.
